units.translation: 1. εἰ with the present indicative, followed in the apodosis by an indicative either expressed or understood, or by an imperative, or by the optative properly so called, or by the optative with ἄν, or by the subjunctive with μή, or by a participle.
With the indicative, followed by the indicative
Followed by the imperative
Followed by the optative
2. With the perfect
3. With the future, followed in the apodosis by the indicative or imperative.
Followed in the apodosis by the optative
4. With the imperfect, followed in the apodosis by the imperfect or aorist with ἄν, used of a thing which is not, but is imagined to be.
Followed in the apodosis by the perfect
5. With the aorist indicative
6. With the optative of a thing which is uncertain whether it is or is not, followed in the apodosis generally by the optative with ἄν.
7. εἰ also with the subjunctive
8. εἰ δὲ μή if not
εἰ μή unless
9. καὶ εἰ even if
10. εἰ if only, would that
11. εἰ in indirect question whether
12. εἰ answered by the particle εἴτε

How this particle differs from ἐάν, which itself also means 'if', has been said under the entry ἐάν. It is a conditional particle, which is constructed with the indicative or optative of all tenses, serving to express a condition, placed either at the beginning or at the end of the sentence, or inserted in the middle of the sentence. Examples of all these are found in countless numbers in any authors you please, so that Wellauer hardly did a worthwhile job when he collected the Aeschylean examples, which I have set out below, after correcting what he had written incorrectly.
and with ἄν omitted
where the apodosis πράσσοιτ᾽ ἂν ὡς ἄριστα [may he fare as well as possible] is to be supplied from the preceding words of the other person.
where εἰ is placed in a double protasis, with the apodosis interposed, as in the Sophoclean passages Ai. 782, El. 582.
With the verb omitted in the apodosis
which is εὐθαρσὴς ἐγὼ ἂν εἴην [I would be confident].
i.e. χάρις ἂν εἴη [it would be a favor].
With anacoluthon

where after εἰ λέγοιμι [if I should say] there should have followed οὐκ ἂν τέλος εὕροιμι [I would not find an end], instead of which is introduced τί δ᾽ οὐ – [why not –]. Similarly at line 563 where χειμῶνα δ᾽ εἰ λέγοι τις οἰωνοκτόνον [if one should speak of a bird-killing storm] and what follows, instead of the apodosis are introduced the words τί ταῦτα πενθεῖν δεῖ; [why must we lament these things?]
